'''Adam Wilhelm Siegmund Günther''' (6 February 1848 – 3 February 1923) was a German geographer, mathematician, historian of mathematics and natural scientist.

==Early life==
Born in 1848 to a German businessman, Günther would go on to attend several German universities including [[Erlangen University|Erlangen]], [[Heidelberg University|Heidelberg]], [[Leipzig University|Leipzig]], [[Berlin University|Berlin]], and [[Göttingen University|Göttingen]].<ref name=mcs>{{cite web|title=Adam Wilhelm Siegmund Günther Biography|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Guenther.html|website=www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk|publisher=School of Mathematics and Statistics University of St Andrews, Scotland|access-date=4 July 2015}}</ref>

==Career==
In 1872 he began teaching at a school in Weissenburg, [[Bavaria]]. He completed his [[habilitation thesis]] on [[continued fraction]]s entitled ''Darstellung der Näherungswerte der Kettenbrüche in independenter Form'' in 1873. The next year he began teaching at [[Munich Polytechnicum]]. In 1876, he began teaching at a university in [[Ansbach]] where he stayed for several years before moving to Munich and becoming a professor of geography until he retired; he served as the university's rector from 1911 to 1913.<ref name=mcs/>

For some years, Günther was a member of the federal parliament, the [[Reichstag (German Empire)|Reichstag]], and later the Bavarian parliament, representing liberal parties.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Daum|title=Wissenschaftspopularisierung|pages=326, 351, 385, 389, 489}}</ref>

His mathematical work<ref name=mcs/> included works on the [[determinant]], [[hyperbolic functions]], and ''parabolic logarithms and trigonometry''.<ref>This is about connecting the ''rectified length'' of line segments along a parabola, giving logarithms for appropriate coordinates, and trigonometric values for suitable angles, in a similar way as the ''area'' under a hyperbola defines the ''[[natural logarithm]]'', and a ''[[hyperbolic angle]]'' is defined via the area of a hyperbolically truncated triangle.</ref>
